summary: Defines a metric for the round-trip delay of packets across Internet paths, which is the time for a packet to go out and the reply to come back.

plainLanguage.summary: A precise way to time a ball thrown to a friend and thrown back.

questions: what is a poisson stream in ippm
subtitle: A precise definition of how to measure the time a packet takes to reach a host and for the reply to return.

tldr.problem: Operators and researchers need a measurement of round-trip delay that is defined so precisely that two different tools measuring it get comparable results.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2681 defines a single measurement (Type-P-Round-trip-Delay), a sample of them taken at Poisson-random times, and statistics such as percentile, median and minimum. It also lists the errors and calibration needed to report results honestly.
tldr.outcome: It gives IPPM measurements a common vocabulary for round-trip time. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 2681 is a Proposed Standard from September 1999, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It defines the round-trip counterpart of the one-way delay metric in RFC 2679.

sections.title: Why Measure Round-trip Delay
sections.content:
RFC 2681 defines a metric for the round-trip delay of packets across Internet paths. It builds on the IPPM Framework (RFC 2330) and follows closely the One-way Delay metric (RFC 2679). The text was largely written by copying material from the one-way document, so similar parts are described with similar words.

The memo moves from a singleton (one observation) to a sample (a sequence of singletons taken at Poisson-process times) to statistics of that sample. The RFC stresses that keeping these three steps separate is important.

The RFC lists why delay matters: some applications perform badly if delay is large, erratic variation hurts interactive real-time applications, and larger delay makes it harder for transport protocols to sustain high bandwidth. The minimum value shows delay due only to propagation and transmission, and values above it indicate congestion on the path.

The RFC is frank that round-trip measurement has weaknesses. The forward and return paths may differ (asymmetric paths), so a round-trip number measures two distinct paths together. Even symmetric paths may queue differently in each direction. An application may depend mostly on one direction, and in networks with quality of service, provisioning may differ per direction.

It also has two advantages. It is easier to deploy, because you can often measure without installing measurement software at the destination, for example with ICMP Echo or TCP-based methods. And it is easier to interpret when the round-trip time is the quantity you actually care about.

Time is measured in seconds relative to UTC. The RFC separates four clock notions: synchronization (two clocks agreeing), accuracy (agreement with UTC), resolution (precision of one clock) and skew (change of accuracy or synchronization over time).
sections.plainLanguage:
Before you can say a road is slow, you need one exact way to time a trip. This RFC picks that way, then builds from one trip to many trips to averages.

Timing a ball thrown there and back is easy because you only need your own watch. But you cannot tell whether the trip out or the trip back was the slow part.

sections.title: The Singleton Metric
sections.content:
The metric is named Type-P-Round-trip-Delay. Its parameters are Src (an IP address), Dst (an IP address) and T (a time). Its value is either a real number of seconds or an undefined (informally, infinite) number.

The delay is dT when Src sent the first bit of a Type-P packet to Dst at wire-time T, Dst received it and immediately sent a Type-P packet back, and Src received the last bit of that packet at wire-time T+dT. It is undefined if Dst did not receive the packet, did not respond, or Src did not receive the response.

Practical points from the discussion: if the response is duplicated, the first instance to arrive sets the delay. If a fragmented packet is not reassembled, it is deemed lost. A method must decide whether a delay is infinite or merely very large, and the RFC mentions the 255 seconds theoretical upper bound on IP packet lifetimes as one simple choice.
sections.plainLanguage: The stopwatch starts when the first bit of your ball leaves your hand and stops when the last bit of the returning ball lands. If the ball never comes back, the time is called infinite.

sections.title: Measuring It in Practice
sections.content:
The method depends on the Type-P (protocol, port, size, precedence). Src builds a test packet and any padding is filled with randomized bits, so compression along the path does not make the delay look lower. The packet must carry identifying information, for example the send timestamp, so the response can be matched.

Src takes a timestamp, sends the packet, and Dst responds as soon as possible. Src takes the final timestamp as soon as it receives the reply, and subtracting gives the estimate. If no response comes within a reasonable period, the delay is taken as undefined, and that threshold is a parameter of the methodology.

You cannot in general add two one-way delay values to get a round-trip value, because the return packet must be triggered by receiving a packet from Src. The RFC says that ping qualifies under this definition, with ICMP echo request and reply and 60-byte packets, but its uncertainties must be analyzed, such as whether a router handles ICMP in the fast path.
sections.plainLanguage: You write the start time on the ball, throw it, and subtract when it comes back. If it takes too long you decide it is lost, and you must say how long "too long" is.

sections.title: Errors, Uncertainty and Calibration
sections.content:
Any specific method must account for sources of error. The RFC names three: clock uncertainty at Src, the difference between wire time and host time, and the time Dst takes to produce a response. A loss threshold can also affect results.

For clocks, round-trip delay needs only that the source clock stays consistent between sending and receiving, not that it be accurate, but a discontinuity such as some NTP adjustments could harm it. A clock with resolution Rsource makes a naive Tfinal-Tinitial off by 2*Rsource. The wire-versus-host uncertainties are Hinitial, Hfinal and Hrefl, and the total bound is 2*Rsource + Hinitial + Hfinal + Hrefl.

Calibration splits a measured value into true value, systematic error and random error. The goal is to find a bound e so that the reported value lies within true value plus or minus e at least 95 percent of the time. The RFC suggests connecting two instruments back to back, repeating the test at least hundreds of times, taking the median as systematic error and the 2.5th to 97.5th percentile range of deviations for the random error. Calibration should use the same measurement load as the field.
sections.plainLanguage: Your stopwatch and your friend are not perfect. You test the stopwatch many times on a very short throw to learn how much it is off, then you say how sure you are of your results.

sections.title: Samples and Poisson Streams
sections.content:
The sample is named Type-P-Round-trip-Delay-Poisson-Stream. Parameters are Src, Dst, T0, Tf and lambda, a rate in reciprocal seconds. A pseudo-random Poisson process of rate lambda picks the times between T0 and Tf, and a singleton is measured at each. The value is a sequence of <time, delay> pairs, which may be empty.

Poisson sampling is used to avoid self-synchronization effects and to get a statistically unbiased sample. The RFC does not claim real traffic is Poisson. It does not fix lambda: too high a rate perturbs the network and causes congestion, too low may miss interesting behavior.

Implementations must handle out-of-order arrival, since a later test packet's response may arrive before an earlier one's. The Framework's Anderson-Darling test can check how well the schedule follows a Poisson process.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of throwing the ball on a fixed beat, you throw at random moments so you never accidentally sync up with something that repeats.

sections.title: Statistics of a Sample
sections.content:
The RFC offers statistics mostly as illustrations. In all of them undefined values count as infinitely large, and an empty sample makes the statistic undefined.

  • Percentile: the Xth percentile of the dT values. For the example 100, 110, undefined, 90 and 500 msec, the 50th percentile is 110 msec.
  • Median: like the 50th percentile, except that with an even number of values it is the mean of the two central ones. The RFC's example gives 105 msec.
  • Minimum: the smallest value, 90 msec in the first example.
  • Inverse percentile: the fraction of values at or below a threshold. In the example, 103 msec gives 50%.
sections.plainLanguage: After many throws, you can report the fastest trip, the middle trip, or how many trips were quicker than some time you care about.

sections.title: What a Report Must Include
sections.content:
Calibration and context MUST be carefully considered and SHOULD always be reported with results. Four items are listed: the exact Type-P (which MUST be reported accurately), the loss threshold or the method that separates a large finite delay from loss (MUST be reported), the calibration results, and the path traversed (SHOULD be reported if possible).

For calibration, any determinable systematic error SHOULD be removed, the calibration error e at 95% confidence SHOULD be reported, and conditions under which finite-delay packets get reported as lost due to instrument resource exhaustion SHOULD be reported if possible. For a stream, the underlying singleton calibration and context MUST be reported with it.
sections.plainLanguage: When you share your times you must also say what kind of ball you used, how long you waited before calling it lost, and how reliable your stopwatch is.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The memo does not specify an implementation, so it does not directly affect Internet security, but implementations must consider two kinds of concern: harm caused by measurements and harm to measurements. Active measurements inject packets, so parameters MUST be chosen so that they add trivial traffic. Too much can skew results and in extreme cases cause congestion and denial of service.

Measurements can be harmed if routers treat measurement traffic differently from normal traffic, or if an attacker injects artificial traffic that is accepted as legitimate, which would artificially lower the loss rate. Methods SHOULD reduce the chance that measurement traffic can be told apart from normal traffic, and authentication such as digital signatures may be used. Privacy concerns are limited because active measurements, unlike passive ones, release no existing user data.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not throw so many balls that you block the playground, and make sure nobody sneaks fake balls in to fool your count.
